A.why_wrong: A dash can’t separate the preposition “from” from its object, “the wood’s surface.”

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, and it can’t separate the preposition “from” from its object.

D.why_wrong: A comma can’t separate the preposition “from” from its object, “the wood’s surface.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (Shiko Munakata, woodblock printmaker, 1956 Venice Biennale print prize). Easy: local preposition-object boundary (1.5, 1.22 menu).

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: Białowieża Forest, which straddles the border between Poland and Belarus, supports one of Europe’s largest populations of European bison. The animals had disappeared from the forest by the early ______ bison raised in captivity were reintroduced there in the 1950s.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence joins two main clauses, “The animals had disappeared from the forest by the early 1920s” and “bison raised in captivity were reintroduced there in the 1950s.” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them and shows the contrast between them.

A.why_wrong: When a coordinating conjunction joins two main clauses of this length, a comma is conventionally placed before it.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses; the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses are fused into a run-on sentence.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Białowieża Forest, European bison reintroduced from captive herds in the 1950s). Easy: comma + but key with the standard splice / fused / conjunction-without-comma trio.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: Pamukkale, a hillside in southwestern Turkey, is covered in brilliant white terraces of a sedimentary stone called travertine. Because the water from the area’s hot springs is rich in dissolved calcium ______ leaves behind a layer of white mineral deposits as it trickles down the slope.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence opens with the dependent clause “Because the water from the area’s hot springs is rich in dissolved calcium carbonate,” which is followed by the main clause “it leaves behind a layer of white mineral deposits as it trickles down the slope.” A comma correctly separates an introductory dependent clause from the main clause.

B.why_wrong: “And” would join the dependent “because” clause to “it leaves behind ...” as if they were parallel, leaving the sentence with no main clause.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “Because the water ... is rich in dissolved calcium carbonate” is a dependent clause.

D.why_wrong: The period makes “Because the water from the area’s hot springs is rich in dissolved calcium carbonate” a separate sentence, but a dependent clause can’t stand alone.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Pamukkale travertine terraces, Turkey). Easy: Because-clause intro (1.6 shape), with the added-and decoy of 1.6 and the strong-mark fragments of 1.8.

items.subtype: Direct question after a colon: inverted order and question mark
items.passage: During some economic downturns, sales of lipstick and other small luxuries have held steady or even increased while spending on big purchases declined. This pattern, sometimes called the lipstick effect, raises a question: Why ______ One explanation is that small treats feel indulgent without costing much.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: do shoppers keep buying small luxuries when money is tight.
shoppers keep buying small luxuries when money is tight?
do shoppers keep buying small luxuries when money is tight?
shoppers keep buying small luxuries when money is tight.
items.explanation: The colon introduces a direct question that begins with “Why.” A direct question puts the helping verb before the subject (“do shoppers keep buying”) and ends with a question mark.

A.recipe: question errors (direct question ending in a period)
A.why_wrong: The word order is that of a direct question, but a direct question must end with a question mark, not a period.

B.recipe: question errors (statement order with a question mark)
B.why_wrong: A direct question introduced by “Why” needs the helping verb “do” before the subject; “shoppers keep buying” is statement order.

D.recipe: question errors (direct question left as a statement)
D.why_wrong: This is statement order with a period, but the text introduces a direct question (“raises a question: Why”), which needs question order and a question mark.

items.notes: Subject: social science and economics (the lipstick effect in recessions). Easy: direct question after a colon (1.18 shape), the full 2 x 2 grid of word order and end mark; a following sentence starts with a capital so the end mark matters.

items.subtype: Comma before a nonrestrictive which clause
items.passage: California grunion have an unusual reproductive strategy: they leave the water to spawn. On spring and summer nights following the highest tides, females wriggle tail-first into wet sand to deposit their ______ hatch approximately ten days later, when the next high tides wash them out to sea.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “females wriggle tail-first into wet sand to deposit their eggs” is followed by a relative clause, “which hatch approximately ten days later ...,” that adds information about the eggs. A comma correctly sets off this supplementary clause from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “which hatch approximately ten days later ...” is a relative clause, not a main clause.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “Which hatch approximately ten days later ...” a separate sentence, but a relative clause can’t stand alone.

D.why_wrong: A colon introduces an explanation or list, not a relative clause that describes “eggs.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (California grunion beach spawning). Easy: trailing which clause (1.32 shape).

items.subtype: Semicolon between independent clauses
items.passage: Fourteenth-century poet Hafez remains one of Iran’s most widely read writers. Many families keep a copy of his collected poems, the Divan, at ______ they consult it on special occasions, opening the book at random and interpreting the poem they find as personal guidance.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence joins two main clauses, “Many families keep a copy of his collected poems, the Divan, at home” and “they consult it on special occasions, opening the book at random and interpreting the poem they find as personal guidance.” A semicolon is used to join two main clauses without a conjunction.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses; the result is a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: When “and” joins two main clauses of this length, a comma is conventionally placed before it; without one, the sentence is not punctuated correctly.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses are fused into a run-on sentence.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Hafez's Divan opened at random for guidance, fal-e Hafez). Easy: semicolon key, menu of 1.4 (comma, no mark, and without comma); second clause opens with a pronoun subject. No period option (it would be a twin).

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long past-participle opener
items.passage: Since 2015, archaeologists beneath Mexico City have been excavating the Huei Tzompantli, the monumental rack on which the Aztecs publicly exhibited the skulls of sacrificial ______ together with lime mortar into a cylindrical tower adjoining the rack, the skulls number in the hundreds, and some belonged to women and children.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence is complete once it reaches “the skulls of sacrificial captives.” The phrase “Bound together with lime mortar into a cylindrical tower adjoining the rack” describes “the skulls,” the subject of the second main clause, which goes on with the verb “number.” A period between “captives” and “Bound” correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: With no mark, “bound together with lime mortar ...” attaches to “captives,” and the main clause “the skulls number in the hundreds” then follows the first main clause after only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: The comma lets the phrase seem to describe the captives, but the main clause “the skulls number in the hundreds” then follows the first main clause after only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “Who were bound ...” keeps the phrase inside the first sentence as a description of the captives, so “the skulls number in the hundreds” still follows a complete main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: archaeology (Huei Tzompantli, Templo Mayor area, excavated by Mexican archaeologists from 2015; skulls set in lime mortar in a tower, women and children among them). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-7 checks: past-participle opener of 11 words (“Bound together ... adjoining the rack”) that reads naturally on clause 1's last noun (“captives bound”); the comma, glued and who-were options hold until the splice at “the skulls number,” 13 words after the blank; one-sentence run of 48 words; cue outside a 6-word window; reasoning steps 3. Key is not the longest option.

comma, glued and who-were options hold until the splice 13 words after the blank
one-sentence run of 48 words

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before an introductory participial phrase
items.passage: In 1917, Dutch astronomer Adriaan van Maanen photographed the spectrum of a faint white dwarf on a glass plate that subsequently remained in an observatory archive for nearly a ______ the plate in 2016, an astronomer identified absorption lines of calcium, an indication that rocky debris had been accumulating on the star.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 1917, Dutch astronomer Adriaan van Maanen photographed the spectrum ... for nearly a century” is a complete sentence. The second sentence opens with the phrase “Reexamining the plate in 2016,” which describes its subject, “an astronomer,” and then gives the verb “identified.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses; “an astronomer identified absorption lines of calcium” is a complete clause, so the sentence becomes a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: “And reexamining” has nothing parallel to join in the first clause, and the main clause “an astronomer identified absorption lines of calcium” is still attached to the first main clause by a comma alone.

C.why_wrong: With no mark, “reexamining the plate in 2016” runs on from “nearly a century,” and the main clause “an astronomer identified absorption lines of calcium” then follows after only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: astronomy (van Maanen's 1917 plate of the white dwarf now called van Maanen 2, reexamined in 2016 and found to show calcium, the earliest record of a metal-polluted white dwarf). Real subject the writer knows; the 2016 astronomer is left unnamed. No fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-6 shape: participial opener of 5 words before clause 2's subject, as in the band-6 models (By dissolving ..., Praising ...). Key is not the longest option.

band7.why: 5-word participial opener before clause 2's subject, as in band-6 aab74a3b and b15724fc; band-6 target, met.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening the second clause: semicolon before, comma after
items.passage: Saxaul, a drought-tolerant shrub with extensive roots and nearly leafless branches, is widely cultivated in Central Asia to prevent migrating dunes from burying highways and farmland. The shrubs do not physically obstruct windblown ______ they reduce the wind’s velocity near the ground, so that airborne grains settle and accumulate around their stems.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The shrubs do not physically obstruct windblown sand” and “they reduce the wind’s velocity near the ground ...” are both main clauses, and “rather” introduces the second one as the correction of the first. A semicolon after “sand” joins the clauses, and a comma after “rather” sets off the adverb at the start of the second clause.

B.why_wrong: Commas around “rather” leave two main clauses joined by a comma alone; a conjunctive adverb cannot join clauses the way a conjunction can.

C.why_wrong: Nothing separates the two main clauses, so “The shrubs do not physically obstruct windblown sand rather, they reduce the wind’s velocity ...” runs them together.

D.recipe: misplaced boundary (adverb on the wrong side)
D.why_wrong: The semicolon puts “rather” at the end of the first clause, where it means nothing; “rather” has to open the clause that gives what the shrubs do instead.

items.notes: Subject: ecology (saxaul, Haloxylon, planted to fix dunes in Central Asia; slows near-ground wind so sand settles around it). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-6 shape modelled on a9e5b788 (`; rather,` after a negated first clause); options vary the semicolon and comma around the adverb. Key is not the longest option (B and D are as long).

band7.why: “; rather,” after a negated first clause is the band-6 shape (a9e5b788); band 7 never uses rather. Strong band 6 as targeted.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing the first clause: comma before, semicolon after
items.passage: In the 1100s, German abbess Hildegard of Bingen compiled roughly 1,000 words of a language she called Lingua Ignota (“unknown language”), inventing names for plants, tools, and ecclesiastical officials. She did not construct a complete ______ the vocabulary consists almost entirely of nouns, which she inserted into sentences that otherwise follow Latin grammar.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “She did not construct a complete language” qualifies the first sentence, which says Hildegard compiled “roughly 1,000 words of a language she called Lingua Ignota,” so “however” belongs with that clause and marks the contrast with the sentence before. The next clause, “the vocabulary consists almost entirely of nouns, which she inserted into sentences that otherwise follow Latin grammar,” explains the qualification. A comma before “however” and a semicolon after it join the two main clauses correctly.

A.why_wrong: Putting “however” at the start of the second clause sets “the vocabulary consists almost entirely of nouns ...” against “She did not construct a complete language,” but the second clause supports the first rather than contrasting with it.

C.why_wrong: Commas around “however” leave two main clauses joined by a comma alone.

D.why_wrong: With no mark after “however,” the main clause “the vocabulary consists almost entirely of nouns ...” runs straight on from the first main clause with nothing to join them.

items.notes: Subject: language (Hildegard of Bingen's Lingua Ignota, a glossary of about 1,000 coined words, mostly nouns, used inside Latin sentences such as the antiphon O orzchis Ecclesia). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-7 checks: the adverb closes clause 1, and clause 1 corrects the previous sentence (a 'language' of coined words is not a complete language); clause 2 elaborates clause 1, so the textbook `; however,` fails only on meaning against the previous sentence; cue outside the 6-word window (the contrast is with the first sentence); logic-wrong distractor present. Key is not the longest option.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1, which qualifies the previous sentence
logic-wrong `; however,` distractor that fails only on meaning
deciding cue in the previous sentence

band7.why: be37d4ae and c06af4d8 shape and menu. The only contrast is with sentence 1 (“compiled roughly 1,000 words of a language”), which the key's clause-1 “however” expresses; clause 2's main predicate, “consists almost entirely of nouns,” is the reason for “did not construct a complete language,” and “which she inserted into sentences that otherwise follow Latin grammar” also supports it, so no contrastive reading of “; however,” survives for a careful student.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a specifying list

items.explanation: “Visitors could order coffee or tea” and “conversation was usually discouraged so that everyone could concentrate on the music” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them, and “but” marks the contrast between what visitors could do and what was discouraged.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the main clauses “Visitors could order coffee or tea” and “conversation was usually discouraged ...” are fused.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses “Visitors could order coffee or tea” and “conversation was usually discouraged ...,” so the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: When “but” coordinates two main clauses such as these, a comma is conventionally used before it.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “Although most of the characters have eroded” is a dependent clause.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “Although most of the characters have eroded” a sentence of its own, but a clause beginning with “although” can’t stand alone; it is a fragment.

items.subtype: Embedded question: statement order and a period
items.passage: Lake-effect snow, which forms when frigid air crosses a relatively warm lake, often falls in narrow bands. To warn the right communities, meteorologists analyze wind patterns to determine where ______ Even a slight shift in wind direction can move a band many kilometers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: does the heaviest snow tend to fall?
the heaviest snow tends to fall?
the heaviest snow tends to fall.
does the heaviest snow tend to fall.
items.explanation: The blank completes an embedded question, “where the heaviest snow tends to fall,” which is the object of “determine.” An embedded question uses statement word order (the subject “the heaviest snow,” then the verb “tends”), and because the sentence as a whole is a statement, it ends with a period.

A.why_wrong: Inverted order with “does” and a question mark would suit a direct question, but this clause is part of the statement “meteorologists analyze wind patterns to determine where ...,” so it takes statement order and a period.

B.recipe: question errors (question mark on a statement)
B.why_wrong: The word order is right for an embedded question, but the sentence is a statement, not a question, so it can’t end with a question mark.

D.recipe: question errors (inverted order in an embedded clause)
D.why_wrong: An embedded question doesn’t use inverted order (“does the heaviest snow tend”); the subject comes before the verb: “the heaviest snow tends.”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “which workers may have rolled along the road to flatten its surface” is a relative clause, not a main clause.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “Which workers may have rolled along the road to flatten its surface” a sentence of its own, but a which clause can’t stand alone; it is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: A colon introduces an explanation or a list, not a which clause that describes the noun before it; a comma is used here.

items.subtype: Opening comma of a nonrestrictive which clause between subject and verb
items.passage: Matrakçı Nasuh, a sixteenth-century Ottoman mathematician and historian, painted the cities that Sultan Suleiman’s army passed through during a military campaign in the 1530s. His city ______ show buildings, rivers, and gardens in meticulous detail, contain no human figures at all.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “which show buildings, rivers, and gardens in meticulous detail” adds information about “His city views,” and the comma after “detail” closes it. A comma before “which” opens the clause to match, so the sentence still reads correctly without it: “His city views contain no human figures at all.”

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, and “His city views” is only the subject; the clause also needs a comma, not a colon, to match the one after “detail.”

B.why_wrong: Without a comma before “which,” the comma after “detail” has no partner, and it ends up separating the subject “His city views” from its verb, “contain.”

C.why_wrong: The period cuts the subject “His city views” off from its verb, “contain,” so neither “His city views.” nor “Which show ... no human figures at all.” is a complete sentence.
